sentences.text: Zhenyuanlong suni was a mid-sized dromaeosaurid covered in a coat of simple filaments over most of its body, with large wings and long tail feathers.

The preserved skeleton measures 122.6 cm in length because the rear half of the tail is missing, though including the long tail feathers, the animal may have reached a total length of 2 meters in life.
Body feathers were preserved only as small impressions on the front and back of the neck, yet the wing feathers were very long, measuring more than twice the length of the upper arm bone.
Zhenyuanlong was roughly the size of a condor but weighed twice as much, at approximately 20 kilograms, making it the largest known non-avian dinosaur with complex feathers.
It is also the first short-legged dromaeosaurid with a feathered morphology.
Zhenyuanlong is known from only one fossil specimen, the holotype JPM-0008, which preserves a nearly complete skeleton with skull and jaws.
The species was named and described in 2015 by paleontologists Lü Junchang and Stephen Brusatte.
Despite having modern-looking wings, Zhenyuanlong was likely too large and heavy to fly or glide, emphasizing the need for biomechanical modeling to determine the function of its wings.
The presence of large wings on a non-flying dromaeosaur raises questions about their function.

Zhenyuanlong is classified within the family Dromaeosauridae, and cladistic analysis places it in the same evolutionary position as other Liaoning dromaeosaurids like Changyuraptor, Graciliraptor, Microraptor, Sinornithosaurus, and Tianyuraptor.

Zhenyuanlong lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Asia, though the genus existed from the Barremian to the Aptian, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.

It is impossible to determine if Zhenyuanlong's body feathers were simple filaments or complex structures with a central vane, and due to preservation issues, the symmetry of the tail feathers cannot be fully assessed, though they resemble those of other bird-like dinosaurs.
Because the tail tip is missing, it cannot be ruled out that Zhenyuanlong had a fan-like structure at the end of its tail.

Researchers suggest that the most viable function for Zhenyuanlong's wings was sexual display, such as threatening rivals or courting mates, similar to how a peacock uses its tail, though alternative hypotheses include protecting eggs in the nest or some form of arboreal gliding.
